---
title: "Acyl chemistry: follow the intermediate"
---

Allow 75–90 minutes. You need carbonyl addition, acid–base arrows and formal
charges. Work on paper first; use the figures to check your bond bookkeeping.

## 1. Find the acyl carbon

Draw CH₃COOH, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, CH₃CONH₂ and CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₃. Circle any carbonyl
carbon. Identify the acid, ester, amide and ether. Explain why an ester oxygen
is part of a different reactive motif from an ether oxygen.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
In the condensed formula CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, the second carbon is C(=O), not a carbon
with two unrelated single-bonded oxygens. Redraw the bonds explicitly.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The first three structures contain CH₃–C(=O)–Y with Y = OH, OCH₂CH₃ or NH₂.
They are acid, ester and amide. The ether contains no carbonyl and no acyl
carbon. The ester can undergo attack at carbonyl carbon followed by leaving-group
loss; the same carbonyl addition step is unavailable to the ether.
:::

## 2. Draw hydroxide addition to an ester

Use ethyl ethanoate, CH₃C(=O)OCH₂CH₃. Draw a lone pair from hydroxide oxygen to
the acyl carbon and move the carbonyl pi pair to oxygen. Draw the resulting
tetrahedral intermediate with **every relevant hydrogen and charge**. Label
the original carbonyl oxygen, incoming oxygen and original ester oxygen.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The intermediate is CH₃C(O⁻)(OH)(OCH₂CH₃). The original carbonyl O is O⁻;
the incoming hydroxide oxygen now has C–O and O–H bonds and is neutral. The
ethoxy oxygen remains neutral with two bonds. Carbon has four single bonds,
and the net charge remains −1. An intermediate retaining C=O as well as both
new and old substituents would give five bonds at carbon and is invalid.
:::

## 3. Finish the hydrolysis and account for the proton

Collapse that intermediate by reforming C=O and breaking the acyl C–OEt bond.
Then show the acid–base step between the initially formed carboxylic acid and
ethoxide. What species predominates in the basic reaction mixture? What does
acid work-up change?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
An ordinary carboxylic acid is much more acidic than ethanol. Do not stop at
an acid and a strongly basic alkoxide coexisting as the final pair.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The O⁻ pair forms a C=O pi bond while the C–OEt pair moves onto ethoxy oxygen.
This gives CH₃COOH and CH₃CH₂O⁻ in the simple stepwise model. Ethoxide removes
the acid proton to give CH₃COO⁻ and ethanol. Overall, ester plus hydroxide gives
carboxylate plus alcohol. Acid work-up protonates carboxylate to the neutral
acid; it does not reverse the atom identities in the product. These are
mechanistic reasoning drawings, not instructions to conduct a reaction.
:::

## 4. Compare aldehyde addition with ester substitution

Draw hydroxide addition to ethanal as a reversible elementary step. Compare
its tetrahedral species with the ester intermediate above. Why is expelling
H⁻ from the ethanal intermediate not a reasonable analogy to loss of ethoxide?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The aldehyde has H where an ester has OR. Hydride would be an extremely poor
leaving group in this setting. An aldehyde can return to its starting carbonyl
by reversing addition or proceed through appropriate addition chemistry; it
does not ordinarily substitute away its carbon-bound H by this analogy.
Product prediction must consider leaving-group viability, not just valence.
:::

## 5. Explain an amide using resonance

Draw neutral ethanamide and its charge-separated contributor with a C=N bond.
Assign O and N charges and count the total charge. Explain why the C–N bond
rotates less freely than a simple amine C–N bond. Then predict the initial
outcome of mixing ethanoic acid with methylamine in water.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The second contributor is CH₃C(O⁻)=NH₂⁺. Net charge stays zero, and the actual
amide has partial C–N double-bond character. Its nitrogen pair is less
available for ordinary protonation than a simple amine pair. Acid plus
methylamine initially gives ethanoate and methylammonium; amide formation
requires appropriate activation or conditions. This is also why peptide
formation in water needs more than simply bringing amino acids together.
:::

## Leave with

A complete ester-hydrolysis mechanism, a comparison with carbonyl addition,
and an explanation of amide properties. Optional reading is selected Solomons
chapter 17; consult the [reading guide](../reference/reading.qmd).
